items.rationale: Any split that would leave fewer than min_samples_leaf training samples in a child is not allowed, so leaves average more rows and predictions smooth out. Confusing it with the minimum samples needed to split a node (min_samples_split) is a typical slip.

Each row is predicted only by the trees whose bootstrap sample left it out, so the OOB score estimates generalization from the training rows alone. Option c describes a held-out test set; OOB needs no separate set, and option b is training error.
n_estimators is the number of trees fitted and averaged into the forest's prediction. Option a describes the bootstrap sample size, a different quantity and the likeliest mix-up.

RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error: a typical error size in the target's units that penalizes large misses more. Option c is mean absolute error, which counts every miss equally; option a is R², which is unit-free; option d is MSE, in squared units.

Leaves of one row mean each tree fits noise, so raising min_samples_leaf regularizes each tree and should raise the OOB score. More trees (option a) already showed no gain, and raising max_features (option c) makes the already correlated trees more alike, weakening the averaging.

For B trees of variance s2 and pairwise correlation r, the average has variance r*s2 + (1-r)*s2/B = 0.5*4 + 0.5*4/100 = 2 + 0.02 = 2.02. An answer of 0.04 assumes uncorrelated trees; correlation puts a floor of r*s2 = 2 under the variance, which is why more trees stop helping and why lowering max_features helps.

Choosing the best of 60 settings by test score makes the test rows part of model selection, so the winning score is biased upward. Option b is wrong because a forest that never trained on the test rows still gives a biased score once those rows picked the winner; option d is wrong because the best of many noisy scores sits above a typical one.

Forest A has squared errors 1, 4, 4 and 16, mean 6.25, RMSE 2.5; forest B has four squared errors of 4, mean 4, RMSE 2.0, so A ranks worse. An answer of 2.25 is A's mean absolute error, and 6.25 forgets the square root.

The best score is 0.873, so the forest must reach at least 0.871; 400 trees scores 0.872 and is the cheapest that qualifies. Option b is tempting because the curve looks flat, but 100 trees scores 0.868, which is 0.005 below the best.
